body.text: Indonesia’s Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka yesterday submitted his resignation, marking an escalation in the destabilizing power struggle between President Prabowo Subianto and his predecessor.

Gibran, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko “Jokowi” Widodo, has come under pressure following Constitutional Court and Supreme Court rulings that found that his education documents did not meet the requirements laid out in Indonesia’s electoral laws.

Citing his aide Budi Arie Setiadi, the BBC reported that Gibran had submitted his resignation letter directly to Prabowo yesterday. Budi said that it was unclear if the president had accepted the resignation.

This follows reports that the two leaders held a two-and-a-half hour meeting at the Widya Chandra housing complex in South Jakarta on Tuesday. This was followed by an announcement from the presidential palace that Gibran had submitted his resignation.

Indonesia’s Supreme Court ruled last week that a high-school equivalency certificate submitted by Gibran as part of his candidacy in the 2024 election – he completed most of his education abroad – was invalid and had been improperly accepted by election officials.
“No evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification,” it said.
This followed a Constitutional Court ruling from earlier in October that came to the same conclusion.

The Supreme Court said that it did not have the power to remove Gibran from office, but earlier this week, members of the House of Representatives sought to initiate a parliamentary inquiry aimed at his impeachment. The vice president’s resignation would be an attempt to get ahead of any attempt to remove him from office; alternatively, he may have forced to resign.

The school credentials controversy is connected to the widening – and now probably unbridgeable – rift between Jokowi and Prabowo. After competing against one another for the presidency in 2014 and 2019, the pair formed an alliance ahead of the 2024 presidential election. In exchange for Jokowi’s support, Prabowo appointed Gibran as his vice-presidential running mate, smoothed by a questionable Constitutional Court ruling that waived the minimum age requirement for the then 36-year-old Gibran.
However, there have been persistent rumors of a split between the two leaders during Prabowo’s two years in office, and as vice president, Gibran has largely been sidelined from state duties.

The dispute seemingly broke into the open last week, with the bombshell announcement that three senior police officials had been arrested for illegally tapping the phones of Prabowo and other prominent politicians, as well as journalists, civil society organizations, and businesspeople. While the exact motivations of the wiretapping remain unclear, among the three arrested were Prabowo’s chief of staff, Listyo Sigit Prabowo – an ally of Jokowi who served as chief of the Indonesian National Police (Polri) until his removal from the post on October 1.

The other two were Inspector General Ahrie Sonta Nasution, the head of Polri’s legal division, and Inspector General Eko Hadi Santoso, a senior instructor at the National Police Education and Training Institute.

As Ary Hermawan, the editor of Indonesia at Melbourne, wrote today, the arrests have been widely seen “as a major escalation in the longstanding power struggle” between Prabowo and Jokowi. This effort has focused on breaking up the influence of Jokowi’s “Solo Gang” – a network of loyalists with connections to his hometown in central Java, which Prabowo fears could pose a challenge to his re-election prospects at the next presidential election in 2029.

In this network, Listyo, also a former police chief of Solo, played a particularly important role. As Ary noted, “his removal was seen by many as the first strike by Prabowo against Jokowi, who is believed to have relied heavily on Listyo and his deep influence within the police.” Gibran’s resignation, voluntary or otherwise, would further deprive the “Solo Gang” of an important asset, he concluded.

There are other signs of shifting political alliances within the government. On Monday, three members of Prabowo’s Cabinet collectively resigned from the Indonesian Solidarity Party (PSI), which is led by Kaesang Pangarep, Jokowi’s youngest son, citing their desire to focus on their duties in Prabowo’s administration. According to some analysts, Gibran’s resignation could be followed by a further flight of the remaining Jokowi loyalists to Prabowo.

The past week’s drama likely marks a final sundering of the political alliance between Jokowi and Prabowo. Dominique Nicky Fahrizal, a researcher at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies in Jakarta, told Nikkei Asia that the current imbroglio could set the stage for the two leaders and their associated networks to renew their electoral rivalry at the 2029 election.

The power struggle between the two leaders also carries hints of a more destabilizing struggle: between the police and the military, two institutions that have vied for power and influence since the fall of Suharto in 1998. Jokowi’s decade in power was a time in which the national police enjoyed relative supremacy, playing a prominent role in internal security operations while high-ranking Polri personnel were appointed to important posts in government and at key state-owned enterprises. The center of political gravity has shifted back toward the military since Prabowo, a former special forces general, took the reins of power in 2024.
Any further escalation of this feud will likely have negative implications for Indonesian democracy and civil liberties – to say nothing of the country’s brittle economy.
